title: Is −1 or 2 a Square mod p?
short: −1 is a square mod an odd prime p exactly when p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and 2 is a square exactly when p ≡ ±1 (mod 8).
trouble: Students use the rule for −1 on 2, or look at p mod 4 when the rule for 2 needs p mod 8.

blocks.html: Euler's criterion decides any single case. For two special numbers, $-1$ and $2$, it gives a rule that depends only on the remainder of $p$ mod 4 or mod 8. These two rules, the supplementary laws, are the base cases of quadratic reciprocity.
Theorem. For an odd prime $p$: $$\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right) = 1 \iff p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}, \qquad \left(\frac{2}{p}\right) = 1 \iff p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{8}.$$

For $-1$: Euler gives $\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right) \equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/2}$, which is $1$ exactly when $\frac{p-1}{2}$ is even, that is, $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$.
For $2$: multiply the even numbers $2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdots (p - 1)$. Factoring out a 2 from each gives $2^{(p-1)/2} \cdot \left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!$. Now replace each even number bigger than $\frac{p}{2}$ by $-(p - \text{that number})$, a negative odd number below $\frac{p}{2}$. The list becomes $\pm 1, \pm 2, \dots, \pm \frac{p-1}{2}$ with one minus sign for each even number above $\frac{p}{2}$. So $2^{(p-1)/2} \equiv (-1)^{m}$, where $m$ counts the even numbers between $\frac{p}{2}$ and $p$, and checking the four cases of $p \bmod 8$ shows $m$ is even exactly when $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{8}$. For $p = 11$: the evens above 5.5 are 6, 8, 10, so $m = 3$ and $\left(\frac{2}{11}\right) = -1$.

head: $p \bmod 8$
blocks.cap: The rule for $-1$ depends on $p$ mod 4; the rule for 2 needs $p$ mod 8. The last row is the product of the two above it.

blocks.title: Is −1 a square?
blocks.q: Find $\left(\frac{-1}{13}\right)$ and a square root of $-1$ mod 13.

blocks.title: Is 2 a square?
steps: $11 \equiv 3 \pmod{8}$, so $\left(\frac{2}{11}\right) = -1$, matching the list of squares mod 11 (2 is not on it).

blocks.html: Using the rule for $-1$ on $2$, or looking at $p$ mod 4 when the rule for 2 needs $p$ mod 8. For $p = 7$: $7 \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, so $-1$ is not a square, but $7 \equiv 7 \equiv -1 \pmod{8}$, so 2 is a square: $3^{2} = 9 \equiv 2$. Keep the two rules separate.
The first law has a famous consequence. If $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, there is an $x$ with $p \mid x^{2} + 1$, and that is the starting point for writing $p$ as a sum of two squares.
$-1$ is a square mod $p$ exactly when $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$; $2$ is a square exactly when $p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{8}$. Products follow by multiplicativity.
